summary:
Mars Base Explorer is a browser-based game where players plan their walk/drive on the Red Planet and simulate the chosen route. It was created for the Martian Map challenge.

The game begins on the globe with nine mission landing sites. Of these, two - Jezero and Gale - can be landed on and give players a 5 km map based on HiRISE 1 m DEM and 25 cm photos. Players choose the destination, and the program calculates several possible routes for an astronaut to follow or for a crew rover. Every route receives a score (Safe, Be careful, Danger or No-go) along with the reasons (slope too high, insufficient suit power, radiation dose, travel time back to shelter, and no radio communication). The map has seven layers showing the grounds for the score (photos, hazards, elevation, radiation, solar power, radio and heat).

After planning you walk or drive the route in 3D on the exact same terrain. The Mars clock ticks away autonomously, the weather is recorded in one sol according to Perseverance or Curiosity’s recordings, and dust and solar storms hit at pre-published frequencies. A card pops up on your screen with the most immediate step to take.

The challenge asks for Mars data from multiple missions in one layered map. Our map layers terrain, imagery, thermal, weather, radiation, and rover traverse data from NASA’s various missions. On Mars, a crew would wait longer than 30 minutes to get a response from Earth, so we wanted our map to show them instantly if a trip is safe and why.
details:
Play the game in your browser (no install, no login): https://mohammadalkurd.github.io/NASA-space-app-challenge/

What it does

The game starts with a globe showing nine mission landing sites. Jezero and Gale, where Perseverance and Curiosity are stationed, can be landed on, and the other seven are just view-only.

In the Plan mode, you select a destination and receive several routes to it, each rated by the game. There are six types: Safest, Fastest, Least effort, Science-rich, Low radiation and In radio range. Of course, you are free to create your own path, too. Each one gives the duration of travel, distance, suit/rover energy left, radiation dose and how far the route runs out of radio sight of the lander. Another tool rates any point as suitable for building a base.

There are seven map layers: Photo, Hazards (slope), Elevation, Radiation shelter, Solar power, Radio line of sight and Heat.

In Explore mode you go around on foot as an astronaut or in a crewed rover in 3D using the same terrain. There is a view from the helmet and a minimap with any layer of your choice. The shelter in this case is the lander.

There are 19 science stops – 9 from Perseverance and 10 from Curiosity. Each science stop provides the image the rover took there.

The Mars Clock runs independently. The temperature, wind, pressure, and dust are based on measurements made during one sol at each site. Solar particle storms, dust storms, and dust devils happen at the published rates.

The game monitors nine safety conditions: solar storm, dust storm, too far from a shelter, suit at turn-back point, dark, extremely cold, wind gusts, steep terrain, and the rover too far away to return by walking. Every rule has the action to take, the reason and the number behind it.

A route can be exported in three formats: printable checklist, GeoJSON, or CSV.

How it works

Using a Python pipeline the elevation and photo mosaics from NASA and USGS are cut into sites. Using the elevation data, the pipeline calculates the slope, sky visibility (used for calculation of radiation shelters), and sun shadow.

The routes are found using a shortest path search of the terrain grid. Speed and energy depend on the slope along the travel direction, and every travel is checked for return to shelter.

Radio coverage is found using a line-of-sight test from the lander antenna over the elevation model, and it takes into account the planet curvature.

The Sources panel within the game categorizes all numbers as Measured, Analog, NASA study or Assumption.

Advantages

A crew would be able to check whether the route is safe or not. They could see the source of any number, and our assumptions would be marked as such.

Tools

For game development we have used TypeScript, three.js, Vite and Playwright, for data – Python with rasterio, NumPy, SciPy and Pillow, and for hosting – GitHub Actions with GitHub Pages.

Limits

Weather is based on the single sol for each site and does not make any forecasts. Radiation at each spot is an estimation calculated based on Curiosity's measurements. The planner ignores rocks which are smaller than its 2.5 m grid size. Radio uses line of sight and no relay satellites are modeled.

AI Usage

Devin (Cognition AI), an AI coding assistant, assisted in writing and testing the code, processing the NASA data files, and drafting the documentation and this text. The team was responsible for directing this process and reviewing the outcome. There are no AI-generated images, videos, audio or 3D objects used in this game. NASA does not endorse this project and the game uses no NASA logos.
